Knesset Inc.: The Closing-Down Sale Before The Vote

The Knesset is in recess. Nobody told the money.

On Tuesday, the Finance Committee approved 267 million shekels ($88 million) in coalition funds. This happened weeks after the government itself dissolved parliament for the October 27 election.

MK Naama Lazimi called it plainly. "Theft from the serving public," she told the committee.

That's not a figure of speech. The package includes 26 million shekels to keep yeshiva students from dropping out, 12.5 million for "Haredi culture," and funding for the Vaad HaYeshivot — an organization whose actual track record is helping young men dodge the draft. Somewhere, a reservist is reading this between rotations.

The same marathon session added another 113 million shekels for settlement expansion. That pushes this year's settlement budget to a record 821 million shekels. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich billed it as funding for "more than 70 archeological and heritage sites".

Activists stormed the hearing room. Committee chairman Hanoch Milwidsky had a warm welcome ready: "a mixed multitude, these are worse than [Nukhba]. Disgusting. Repulsive". Comparing protesters to the Hamas unit that carried out the October 7 massacre is one way to change the subject from a budget line item.

Hiddush and Lazimi tried the courts instead. They asked the Supreme Court to block the meeting before it started. Justice Alex Stein declined. "I did not see fit to grant interim relief," he ruled. Then he ordered the petitioners to report back by 9 a.m. Wednesday on exactly what got approved.

The court can always read the receipt after checkout. Eighty-four days before an election, the recess is decorative, the cash register stays open, and the only oversight in the room is a judge who'll get back to you in the morning.

So who's actually on recess here — the Knesset, or the rule of law?

ONE BILL WILL NOT DEFINE THE ENTIRE MARKET.

The Crypto CLARITY Act remains one of the most important regulatory developments for the US digital asset industry.

The Senate Banking Committee advanced the legislation in May by a bipartisan 15–9 vote.

But the bill has not yet passed the full Senate and has not become law.

At the same time, the regulatory process is not standing still.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins has said that the Commission’s 2026 agenda includes:

• clearer rules for crypto capital formation
• bringing more digital asset products onshore
• custody guidance
• rules for trading tokenized securities onchain

This creates two parallel processes.

Congress can establish a permanent statutory framework and define agency authority.

Regulators can interpret existing laws and develop rules inside the authority they already have.

Those processes are connected.

They are not interchangeable.

Agency rulemaking cannot automatically replace legislation.

Legislation cannot implement itself without detailed regulatory work.

For digital asset companies, the important questions are therefore broader than:

“Will the CLARITY Act pass this week?”

They include:

• What rules are already changing?
• Which agency currently has authority?
• What requires new legislation?
• Which obligations will depend on future rulemaking?
• How long will implementation take after passage?

A headline can create momentum.

A functioning market structure requires:

- law

- rules

- implementation

- enforcement

Legislation defines the architecture.
Regulation turns it into an operating system.

DIY Sweetened Golden Dry Fruit Milk

Ingredients  
1/3 cup almonds, cashews, and pistachios  
1/4 tsp nutmeg powder and 1/4 tsp cardamom powder  
A pinch of saffron  
1 cup milk (dairy or vegan), 10 oz (300 ml)  
Chopped pistachios for garnish  
1/2 tsp turmeric  
Sugar to taste  

Preparation  
Combine the dry fruits, cardamom, nutmeg, and saffron. Grind into a fine, non-sticky powder. Avoid over-processing.  

Add 2 tablespoons of the powder to boiling milk. Stir in sugar and turmeric.  
Reduce heat and simmer gently for 15–20 minutes.  

Pour into a mug.  
Garnish with chopped pistachios and a hint of saffron. Serve warm and enjoy.
